title: What the literal prints
intro: A String literal is the text between double quotes. Inside it, a backslash starts an escape: `\n` is one character (a new line), `\"` is a quote that doesn't end the literal, and `\\` is one backslash. Predict what each line prints.

rounds.right: `\n` is one character, a new line, so the text breaks onto a second line. The String holds {length} characters, though {typed} were typed between the quotes.

why.raw: `\n` is an escape: the backslash and the `n` together make one character, a new line. Java never prints the backslash.
why.quotes: The quotes only mark where the literal starts and ends in your code. They are not part of the text, so `println` doesn't show them.

rounds.right: Each `\"` became one quote character inside the text: the backslash only tells Java that this quote doesn't end the literal.

why.raw: `\"` is one character, a quote. The backslash only tells Java that this quote doesn't end the literal; it isn't printed.
why.quotes: The outer quotes only mark where the literal starts and ends. The quotes that print are the escaped ones inside.

rounds.right: Two backslashes in the code make one backslash in the String: `\\` is an escape like the others.

why.raw: `\\` is an escape too: two backslashes in the code make one backslash in the String, and only that one is printed.
why.quotes: The quotes only mark where the literal starts and ends in your code; `println` shows the text between them.

rounds.right: Escape each quote inside the text with a backslash, and the literal holds exactly what you want printed.

why.naive: The second `"` ends the literal early, and Java can't make sense of what follows: this line doesn't even compile.
why.double: Here each `\\` is an escaped backslash, so the backslashes would be printed along with the quotes.
